title: Apple Watch readiness score: how it works
summary: An example formula, how WHOOP and other wearables differ, and what a study of professional golfers found.
body_markdown:
Apple just announced a Readiness app for Apple Watch, joining a category popularized by WHOOP’s Recovery score. These apps turn overnight measurements into an estimate of how recovered you are, with the idea that you’d work out harder on days with a higher recovery score.


*iOS 27’s new readiness screen shows a score of 7 (“Ready”), with fitness, overnight vitals, and sleep score listed under “Raising Your Score.”*


Most wearable readiness scores use the same inputs—generally[heart rate variability, resting heart rate, sleep, and other signals](https://support.whoop.com/s/article/WHOOP-Recovery?language=en_US) compared to your personal baseline—roughly like so:


Readiness=50+10zHRV−5zresting HR+5zsleep\\text{Readiness} = 50 + 10z_{\\text{HRV}} - 5z_{\\text{resting HR}} + 5z_{\\text{sleep}}

Here, **z** is how far last night’s reading was from your previous 30-night average, divided by its standard deviation (your usual fluctuation). (This is an invented teaching example, not a validated formula or a reconstruction of WHOOP’s or Apple’s algorithm.)


## Are readiness scores actually validated?


Studies that evaluate the accuracy of readiness scores are unfortunately pretty thin. One[study of 389 male professional golfers](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41265431/) analyzed 35,140 nights of wearable data across 521 events. A 10-point higher average WHOOP Recovery score was associated with 0.48 fewer strokes per round between golfers; within the same golfer, a season with a 10-point higher average Recovery was associated with **0.24 fewer strokes** . Both associations were statistically significant.


Trials of HRV-guided training (the basis of commercial readiness scores, but no one company’s proprietary score) provide some encouragement. In[40 runners](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26909534/) , HRV guidance produced a small advantage with fewer hard sessions. But then[meta-analysis of eight studies](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34489178/) found no statistically significant pooled advantage for performance or peak oxygen uptake. So different studies tell us different things.


So take readiness scores with a grain of salt.


## How is Apple’s recovery score different than Whoop, Bevel, and Athlytic?


Apple’s screenshot suggests a familiar idea—combining sleep and overnight physiology into a daily readiness score. But, it explicitly highlights recent fitness activity alongside overnight vitals and sleep score. Apple’s new recovery feature is similar to[WHOOP](https://support.whoop.com/s/article/WHOOP-Recovery?language=en_US) ,[Bevel](https://help.bevel.health/en/articles/11258177) , and[Athlytic](https://athlyticapp.helpscoutdocs.com/article/20-understanding-recovery) , which incorporate HRV, resting heart rate, and more. Apple hasn’t yet revealed the formula for their recovery score, so we’ll update this post as more information becomes available.


## Appendix: known readiness formulas and calculation details


**The documentation below doesn’t disclose a complete formula for any of these four commercial scores.** It identifies inputs, time windows, and some intermediate calculations. Numerical weights and the final mapping to a score remain undisclosed in these sources. A[2025 review of 14 wearable scores](https://doi.org/10.1515/teb-2025-0001) also identified gaps in algorithm transparency.


Score Published calculation details What’s missing for reproduction


[WHOOP Recovery](https://support.whoop.com/s/article/WHOOP-Recovery?language=en_US) HRV and resting heart rate are the biggest contributors. HRV is compared with a 30-day baseline. Other inputs include sleep, breathing rate, temperature, blood oxygen, and cycle context where applicable. Numerical weights, input transformations, and final scoring function.


[Oura Readiness](https://support.ouraring.com/hc/en-us/articles/360057791533-Readiness-Contributors) Nine contributors: resting heart rate, HRV balance, temperature, recovery index, sleep, sleep balance, sleep regularity, previous-day activity, and activity balance. HRV balance compares a weighted 14-day average with a three-month average. Daily averaging weights, contributor-to-points mappings, and final combination.


[Garmin Training Readiness](https://www8.garmin.com/manuals/webhelp/GUID-9D99A9D4-467A-4F1A-A0EA-023184FEA3DD/EN-AU/GUID-C21BE0C8-A08E-4DA1-B6C6-2E0E2DDDB372.html) Combines last night’s sleep score, recovery time, HRV status, acute load, three-night sleep history, and three-day stress history. Updates throughout the day. Weights, interactions, and conversion to the 1–100 score. This isn’t Garmin’s separate Body Battery metric.


[Fitbit / Pixel Watch readiness](https://support.google.com/googlehealth/answer/14236710?hl=en-GB) Combines HRV, resting heart rate, and recent sleep against a personal baseline. Initial calibration requires seven nights. Resting heart rate replaced the older activity component. Weights, normalization, and final scoring function.
